children: The Czech central bank (CNB) left its main repo rate (CZCBIR=ECI) unchanged at 3.75% on Thursday, as expected, but said a hike would be considered at the next meeting in November.
The bank highlighted inflation risks but also that it is in a comfortable position with rates standing well above inflation,  which stood at 1.9% in August, below the bank's target of 2%.
It raised the repo rate by 25 basis points in June, the first increase in four years, and held policy steady in August.
"The rate increase in June has so far led to a sufficient tightening of monetary conditions," Governor Ales Michl said while presenting the board's statement.
He said higher long-term market rates had further tightened financial conditions, with Czech yields influenced by US markets and Federal Reserve policy. The Fed raised rates on Wednesday.

However, Michl said risks to inflation remained tilted to the upside, citing domestic lending growth, wage pressures, wider budget deficits and rising services prices. He said the bank stood ready to tighten policy further if needed.
"At its next meeting, the Bank Board will decide between keeping interest rates unchanged and raising them," Michl said.

He added that fuel prices were contributing to inflationary pressures and that the bank would assess the impact of the Middle East conflict, which has disrupted shipping, although policymakers focused mainly on domestic risks.
A Reuters poll last week showed all 11 analysts expected the bank to keep rates unchanged, while only two of eight forecast a 25-basis-point increase before the end of the year.
A budget deficit expected to rise to around 3.5% of GDP next year also points to inflationary pressures.

Despite that, Prime Minister Andrej Babis has repeatedly called for lower rates. When asked about those comments, Michl reiterated that the next policy debate would be between holding rates steady and raising them.

Another temporary factor is the expiry of an energy-subsidy base effect, which reduced inflation by about 0.4 percentage points this year. When that drops out of annual comparisons in January, inflation is expected to move above 3% in early 2027.
The bank's next policy meeting is scheduled for November 5, when it will also review updated quarterly economic forecasts.

Market rates have risen across the yield curve, with short-term markets pricing in as many as four rate increases over the next year. Some central bankers have said that expectation is overdone and reflects factors beyond the likely path of monetary policy.
